pron:dat.tx: A regional form adopted into colloquial standard German. In western Germany from Central Franconian dat, from northern Middle High German dat, from northern Old High German that, dat, an unshifted relict form possibly due to Frankish influence. In northern Germany from German Low German dat, from Middle Low German dat, from Old Saxon that.

noun:Dezember.tx: Inherited from Middle High German december.

adj:dick.tx: From Middle High German dicke, from Old High German dicki, dicchi (akin to Old Saxon thikki), from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwī. Compare Low German dick, Dutch dik, English thick, Danish tyk.

noun:DNA.tx: Borrowed from English DNA, from deoxyribonucleic acid. Replacing DNS from the calque Desoxyribonukleinsäure.

adv:dar.tx: Inherited from Old High German dār. See dar-. Doublet of da.

pron:du.tx: From Middle High German du, duo, dū, from Old High German dū (akin to Old Saxon thū and English thou), itself from Proto-West Germanic *þū, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

prep:dank.tx: From the noun Dank, as in phrases like "Dank sei dir", with the copula dropping away and a semantic broadening to cover causal senses. Compare English thanks to.

det:der.tx: From Middle High German dër, from Old High German dër, replacing the original masculine and feminine nominative forms from Proto-Germanic *sa, by analogy with the adjective inflection. Compare also Old Dutch thie and Old English sē where the same process occurred. Cognate with Yiddish דער (der).

pron:der.tx: From Middle High German dër, from Old High German dër, replacing the original masculine and feminine nominative forms from Proto-Germanic *sa, by analogy with the adjective inflection. Compare also Old Dutch thie and Old English sē where the same process occurred. Cognate with Yiddish דער (der).

pron:das.tx: From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Silesian East Central German doas, Dutch dat, English that. Doublet of dass. Distinction from dass is purely orthographical convention.

adv:da.tx: From a merger of three interrelated adverbs: 1.) Middle High German dā, dār (“there, at that place”), from Old High German thār, dār, from Proto-West Germanic *þār. 2.) Middle High German dar, dare (“thither, to that place”), from Old High German thara, dara, from an extended form of the former. 3.) Middle High German dō, duo (“then, at that time”), from Old High German thō, dō, duo, from …

conj:da.tx: From a merger of three interrelated adverbs: 1.) Middle High German dā, dār (“there, at that place”), from Old High German thār, dār, from Proto-West Germanic *þār. 2.) Middle High German dar, dare (“thither, to that place”), from Old High German thara, dara, from an extended form of the former. 3.) Middle High German dō, duo (“then, at that time”), from Old High German thō, dō, duo, from …

adj:deutsch.tx: Inherited from Middle High German diutisch, diutsch, tiutsch, from Old High German diutisk (“popular, vernacular”), from Proto-West Germanic *þiudisk, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of the people, popular”), an adjective from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”, whence Old English þeod, Icelandic þjóð), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂. Cognate with Dutch Duits and Diets, Low German düütsch, …

intj:danke.tx: Ellipsis of ich danke dir (“I thank you”).

adv:davon.tx: From Middle High German dāvon, darvon, dar von, equivalent to da + von. Cognate with Dutch daarvan.

det:dein.tx: From Middle High German dīn, from Old High German dīn. Akin to Old Saxon thīn, English thine, thy.

conj:denn.tx: From Middle High German denne, tenne, from Old High German denna, a variant of danne, from Proto-West Germanic *þan. Doublet of dann. The functional split between denn and dann was prescribed only by the grammarians of the 18th century. Cognate with English then and than.

adv:denn.tx: From Middle High German denne, tenne, from Old High German denna, a variant of danne, from Proto-West Germanic *þan. Doublet of dann. The functional split between denn and dann was prescribed only by the grammarians of the 18th century. Cognate with English then and than.

num:drei.tx: From Middle High German drī, from Old High German dri, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Dutch drie, English three, Danish tre.

adj:diagonal.tx: From Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”).

conj:dass.tx: From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Dutch dat, Low German dat, datt, English that. Doublet of das. Distinction from das is purely orthographical convention.

pron:det.tx: Borrowed from Low German det and dät.

noun:Drache.tx: From Middle High German trache, from Old High German trahho, from Proto-West Germanic *drakō, borrowed from Latin dracō. The modern initial d- is influenced by the original Latin, reinforced by dialectal German forms.

adj:doll.tx: Occasionally found in older texts, but chiefly introduced to standard German during the 20th century from Central German and German Low German dialects, from northern Middle High German dol and Middle Low German dol, from Old Saxon dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz. Doublet of toll (“great; crazy”), which compare.

adv:doll.tx: Occasionally found in older texts, but chiefly introduced to standard German during the 20th century from Central German and German Low German dialects, from northern Middle High German dol and Middle Low German dol, from Old Saxon dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz. Doublet of toll (“great; crazy”), which compare.

pron:dey.tx: Borrowed from English they, adjusted to German phonology and suppleted with plural forms of demonstrative pronoun die. dem, demm are borrowed from English them.

adv:dito.tx: From Late Middle High German ditto (15th c.), from older Italian ditto, variant of detto (past participle of dire (“to say”)). The spelling dito, possibly influenced by Venetan dito, appears in German already in the 17th century and thus apparently earlier than French dito (18th c.), though this last may have reinforced it later on.

adv:dort.tx: From Middle High German dort, from Old High German doret, dārot (“thither”), from Proto-West Germanic *þārud (“thither”).

adj:dünn.tx: From Middle High German dünne, from Old High German dunni, from Proto-West Germanic *þunnī. Middle High German -u-, -ü- before nasal geminates regularly become -o-, -ö- in modern German, but for some reason the form dönn(e), though attested, remained very rare.

noun:Dienstag.tx: Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dingesdach, dinsdach and Middle Dutch dinsendach (both with variants), and gradually replaced Middle High German ziestac and other High German forms like Alemannic German Zischtig or Bavarian Ertag. Only since the second half of the 17th. century is the modern form in common Script usage. Probably from Proto-Germanic *þingas-dagaz (“Day of …

noun:Donnerstag.tx: From Middle High German donerstac, from Old High German donarestag, thonarestag (11th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”). Compare Bavarian Dunnersdåg, Low German Dunnersdag, Dutch donderdag, West Frisian tongersdei, English Thursday, Danish torsdag.

adj:dumm.tx: From Middle High German tump, from Old High German tumb, from Proto-West Germanic *dumb, from Proto-Germanic *dumbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dumb, dumm, from Old Saxon dumb). The rare literary variant tumb is a poetic archaism directly borrowed from Middle High German; the expected form of this source is …

noun:Dolch.tx: Uncertain. First attested in the mid-15th century in Upper German texts as Dolch, then also Dollich, Tolch. At first mostly with weak declension (dem Dolchen). The formerly held assumption of a Slavic origin has been abandoned (older Czech tulich is instead a German borrowing). The word is now mostly derived ultimately from Latin dolo (“pike, dagger”), but the origin of the velar remains unclear. …

noun:Diplom.tx: Borrowed from Latin diploma. First attested in the 17th century.

noun:Dilemma.tx: From Latin dilēmma, Ancient Greek δίλημμα (dílēmma)

noun:Dachshund.tx: 15th c., from Dachs (“badger”) + Hund (“dog”), because the breed was used for hunting badgers.

noun:Dame.tx: From French dame, from Latin domina (“mistress, lady”). Cognate with English dame.

noun:Dank.tx: From Middle High German danc, from Old High German danc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz. Compare Dutch dank, English thank, Danish tak. More at thank.

noun:Darmstadtium.tx: Named after the German city Darmstadt, where it was first synthesized, + Latin -ium.

noun:Deal.tx: Borrowed from English deal. Doublet of Teil.

noun:Deck.tx: From Dutch dek. Borrowed via German Low German Deck and hence with a plural in -s (Dutch uses dekken). The older Low German form is preserved in Verdeck. Cognate with English deck.

noun:Decke.tx: From Middle High German decke, from Old High German theckī, decchī, derived from thecken (modern decken), from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Cognate with English deck. Compare analogous Dutch dek. Also related with German Dach, Dutch dak, English thatch.

noun:Demonstration.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin dēmōnstrātio, since the mid 16th century. The military sense developed perhaps under the influence of Italian dimostrazione in the mid 18th century. The rally sense developed under the influence of English demonstration in the mid 19th century.

noun:Deportation.tx: From the 16th century, from Latin dēportātiō.

noun:Design.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English design; cognate with French dessin.

noun:Despot.tx: From Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”)

noun:Dessert.tx: Borrowed from French dessert, from French desservir (“(to) serve”), from Latin dēserviō, dēservīre.

noun:Dialog.tx: From Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos).

noun:Diamant.tx: From Middle High German dīemant, dīamant, dīamante, borrowed from Old French diamant.

noun:Diesel.tx: Named after Rudolf Diesel (1858–1913), the inventor of the Diesel motor. The surname is a variation of Tüssel.

noun:Diktator.tx: From Latin dictātor (“a chief magistrate”), from dictō (“dictate, prescribe”), from dīcō (“say, speak”).

noun:Dill.tx: With Central German consonantism from Middle High German tille, from Old High German tilli, from Proto-West Germanic *dili.

noun:Division.tx: Borrowed from Latin dīvīsiō in the arithmetical sense and from French division in the military sense.

noun:Dock.tx: Borrowed from Dutch or English dock, or via German Low German from Middle Low German docke. Possibly borrowed from Middle English dock; this form is attested a few decades earlier and the earliest Low German attestation refers to the harbours of London. The ultimate origin is uncertain; possibly from Vulgar Latin *ductia (“aqueduct”), from Latin duco (“to lead”).

noun:Dogge.tx: First borrowed as Dock from early modern English dog, dogge (from Old English docga, Old English dogga). Later, the Middle Low German form with -gg- became the accepted form (borrowed from the same English source). Compare Dutch dogge.

noun:Dollar.tx: From English dollar, from early modern Dutch daler (contemporary daalder), from Middle Low German daler, from early modern German Taler. Doublet of Taler

noun:Dom.tx: 15th-century alteration (see below) of older Thum, from Middle High German and Old High German tuom, from Proto-West Germanic *dōm (whence Old Dutch duom, Middle Low German dôm), from Medieval Latin domus (literally “house”). The use probably goes back to domus episcopatus/episcopalis (“house of the bishopric”). An alternative theory derives it from domus ecclesiae (“church house”), after Ancient …

noun:Domain.tx: Borrowed from English domain. Doublet of Domäne.

noun:Donner.tx: From Middle High German doner, donre, donder (also -u-), from Old High German thonar, donar, *duner (attested in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *þunr. Cognate with Dutch donder, English thunder.

noun:Doppelgänger.tx: From earlier Doppeltgänger. Coined by Jean Paul in 1796 in his novel Siebenkäs. By surface analysis, doppel- (“double”) + Gänger (“goer”).

noun:Dose.tx: Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dōse and Middle Dutch dose. Probably from Latin dosis (“dose”), with semantic shift "a small amount (dose) of medicine" > "a container of such a dose of medicine" > "containers in general".

noun:Drama.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “play, drama”, noun), from δρᾰ́ω (drắō, “do, act”, verb) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominalizing suffix). First attested in the 16th century.

noun:Dreck.tx: From Middle High German drëc, from Old High German drec, from Proto-West Germanic *þraki. Cognate with Old Norse þrekkr and Swedish träck.

noun:Dung.tx: From Middle High German tunc, tunge, from Old High German tung, tunga, from Proto-West Germanic *dungu, from Proto-Germanic *dungō, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ- (“to cover”). The word also meant in High German—and it seems exclusively in Low German (compare Old Saxon dung)—a dwelling or storage room (originally under the earth and covered with dung), from Proto-West Germanic *dung …

noun:Dynamo.tx: After English dynamo, from dynamo-electric machine, itself from German dynamoelektrische Maschine, coined by Werner von Siemens, based on Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”).

noun:Deklination.tx: From Latin dēclīnātiō, from dēclīnāre, equivalent to deklinieren + -ation.

noun:Dach.tx: Inherited from Middle High German dach, from Old High German dah, from Proto-West Germanic *þak, from Proto-Germanic *þaką, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg-. Cognate with German Low German Dack, Yiddish דאַך (dakh), Dutch dak, Afrikaans dak, English thack, thatch, Danish tag, Norwegian Bokmål tak, Norwegian Nynorsk tak, Swedish tak, Polish stóg, Belarusian стог (stoh), Ukrainian стіг …

noun:Dreieck.tx: From drei + Ecke. Displaced non-native Triangel, from Latin triangulum.

noun:Daten.tx: Adapted from older Data + -en, replacing it mid-late 19th century.

adv:derbe.tx: Initially a regional variation of derb, popularized via hip-hop culture.

noun:Dünnschiss.tx: dünn (“thin”) + Schiss (“shit”); from the thin, watery consistency of the fecal matter.

noun:Durchfall.tx: Deverbal of durchfallen (“to fall through”) as a calque of Ancient Greek δῐᾰ́ρροιᾰ (dĭắrrhoiă).

verb:denken.tx: From Middle High German denken, from Old High German denken, thenken, from Proto-West Germanic *þankijan, from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng-. Cognate with Bavarian denkn, denka, Dutch denken, dinken, Low German denken, dinken, West Frisian tinke, English think, Icelandic þekkja, Yiddish דענקען (denken).

noun:Dolmetscher.tx: From Middle High German tolmetsche (13th c.), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tilmač (compare Turkish dilmaç). Probably borrowed through a Slavic language; compare Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь (“interpreter”), whence Russian толма́ч (tolmáč), Polish tłumacz. Alternatively through Hungarian tolmács.

adv:damit.tx: From da + mit. Compare English theremid, therewith, Dutch daarmee, Swedish därmed, Icelandic þar með.

conj:damit.tx: From da + mit. Compare English theremid, therewith, Dutch daarmee, Swedish därmed, Icelandic þar með.

noun:Droge.tx: From French drogue, from Middle French circa 1462, from Middle Dutch droge (Modern Dutch droog).

noun:Demokratie.tx: Borrowed from French démocratie, from Medieval Latin dēmocratia (Late 16th century), from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā), equivalent to Ancient Greek δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + -kratie.

noun:Demokrat.tx: Borrowed from French démocrate. First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Dasselfliege.tx: Probably from Low German dase (“stinging fly”).

noun:Dromedar.tx: From Middle High German dromedār (also drummeldar, trummeltier etc.), from Medieval Latin dromedarius (in part through Old French dromedaire), derived from Ancient Greek δρομάς (dromás, “running”). Doublet of Trampeltier.

verb:drucken.tx: From Middle High German drucken, from Old High German drucchen, drukken, from Proto-West Germanic *þrukkijan (“to press”). Doublet of drücken (“to press, push”) with Upper German lack of umlaut before a velar geminate; the first German printers were in the south. Established as technical term for printing in the 17th century (see also bedrucken).

noun:Druck.tx: Inherited from Middle High German druc, from Old High German thruc, equivalent to a deverbal from drücken.

noun:Dachs.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German dahs, from Proto-West Germanic *þahs.

noun:Dackel.tx: Upper German short form for now archaic Dachshund, from Dachs (“badger”) + Hund (“dog, hound”), from the use of the breed for hunting badgers. First attested in the 19th century, but perhaps older; see Teckel.

num:dreizehn.tx: From Middle High German dreizehen, from Old High German drīzehan, akin to Old Saxon thriutein. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þritehun. Equivalent to drei + zehn. Compare Dutch dertien, West Frisian trettjin, English thirteen, Danish tretten.

noun:Drüse.tx: From Middle High German drüese, alongside druose, druos, from Old High German druos (“swelling, swollen gland”). The gender and stem form of the Old High German are uncertain. It was probably a masculine, so the later forms in -e continue plural forms. Alternatively (or additionally) it may have been a feminine i-stem, in which case drüese continues the plural and oblique singular; druose (whence …

adj:dunkel.tx: From Middle High German tunkel, from Old High German tunkal, tuncal (“dark”), from Proto-Germanic *dunkalaz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʷ- (“to smoke, fume”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dunker, also dunkel). Cognate to Dutch donker (“dark”).

noun:Drossel.tx: From Middle High German droschel, from Old High German throskela, from Proto-West Germanic *þrosklā, *þrostlā (“thrush”).

adv:dann.tx: From Middle High German dann, from Old High German danne, from Proto-West Germanic *þan. Cognate with English then.

verb:dienen.tx: From Middle High German dienen, from Old High German dionōn, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōną.

prep:durch.tx: From Middle High German durch, from Old High German duruh, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw. Cognate with English through, thorough, Dutch door, West Frisian troch, Yiddish דורך (durkh).

adv:durch.tx: From Middle High German durch, from Old High German duruh, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw. Cognate with English through, thorough, Dutch door, West Frisian troch, Yiddish דורך (durkh).

adj:durch.tx: From durchgeknallt, durch den Wind, durchdrehen, or another similar expression.

noun:Dunkelziffer.tx: From dunkel (“uncertain”, literally “dark”) + Ziffer (“figure”, literally “digit”). First used in 1908 in the PhD thesis Unverbesserliche Verbrecher und ihre Behandlung (p. 28) of Shigema Oba, a Japanese jurist who moved in 1905 to Germany to study Western law; supposedly based on English *dark-number, but this word is not attested. (English dark figure is calqued from German.)

noun:Dekoration.tx: From French décoration, from Latin decoratio.

adv:doch.tx: From Middle High German doch, from Old High German doh, from Proto-West Germanic *þauh, from Proto-Germanic *þauh. Cognate to Old English þēah (English though).

conj:doch.tx: From Middle High German doch, from Old High German doh, from Proto-West Germanic *þauh, from Proto-Germanic *þauh. Cognate to Old English þēah (English though).

noun:Dorf.tx: From Middle High German dorf, from Old High German dorf, thorph, from Proto-West Germanic *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą. Doublet of Truppe (English troop). Cognate with Old Dutch thorp (modern Dutch dorp), Old Saxon thorp, Old English þorp (archaic English thorp).

noun:Draht.tx: From Middle High German drāt (“wire, thread”), from Old High German drāt, thrāt, from Proto-West Germanic *þrādu, from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *treh₁-tu-, from *terh₁- (“rub, twist”). Related to drehen (“to turn, twist”), with which it was still associated in early modern German, as is proved by the insertion of the lengthening -h- (which is only used before sonorants or …

adj:doof.tx: From German Low German doof (“deaf”), from Middle Low German dôf, from Old Saxon dof, from Proto-West Germanic *daub. Cognate to Upper German taub.

pron:dieser.tx: Inherited from Middle High German diser/dirre, disiu, diz, from Old High German dësēr, disiu, diz, from the Old High German demonstrative pronoun dër, from Proto-Germanic *sa, from Proto-Indo-European *tód. Akin to Old Saxon these.

verb:dürfen.tx: From Middle High German durfen, dürfen, from Old High German durfan, from Proto-West Germanic *þurban, cognate with Ancient Greek τέρπω (térpō, “I delight, please”), English tharf. See können for the origin of the historically unexpected umlaut.

verb:danken.tx: From Middle High German danken, from Old High German dankōn. Compare Dutch danken, English thank, Danish takke.

verb:decken.tx: From Middle High German decken, from Old High German decchen, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan. Equivalent to Dach + -en. Cognate with West Frisian dekke, Dutch dekken, English thatch, Danish tække, Swedish täcka.

noun:Dieb.tx: From Middle High German diep, Old High German diob, from Proto-West Germanic *þeub, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz. Cognate with Old Norse þýfð, Old English þēof, Dutch dief, English thief, Gothic 𐌸𐌹𐌿𐍆𐍃 (þiufs).

noun:Ding.tx: From Middle High German ding, from Old High German thing, from Proto-West Germanic *þing. Compare Low German ding, Dutch ding, English thing, Danish ting.

adj:dritte.tx: From Old High German dritto, akin to Old Saxon thriddio. Equivalent to drei + -te.

noun:Durst.tx: From Middle High German durst, from Old High German durst, thurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”). Akin to Old Dutch thursti (modern dorst), Old English þurst (modern thirst), and Old Saxon thurst.

num:dreißig.tx: From Middle High German drīzic, from Old High German drīzzug, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz. Equivalent to drei + -zig.

noun:Distel.tx: From Middle High German distel, from Old High German distil, from Proto-West Germanic *þistil, from Proto-Germanic *þistilaz, which see for cognates. The alternative long-vowel pronunciation is based on Middle Low German dîstel (alongside distel), whose length is unexplained (cf. the same in Middle Dutch diestel, Early Modern Dutch dijstel).

verb:dulden.tx: From Middle High German dulten, dulden, from Old High German dulten, thulten, derived from thult, githult (compare modern Geduld), a verbal abstract of tholēn from Proto-Germanic *þulāną (“to bear, to endure”). The denominal verb forms are originally south-western and spread northward during the Middle Ages (compare Dutch dulden from Middle Dutch gedult). The second -d- is due to voicing after a …

noun:Dorn.tx: From Middle High German dorn, from Old High German dorn, from Proto-West Germanic *þornu, from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter- (“stiff”). Compare Low German Doorn; Durn (Mecklenburgisch-Vorpommersch); Däörn (Münsterländisch), Dutch doorn, English thorn, Danish torn, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌽𐌿𐍃 (þaurnus).

verb:dreschen.tx: From Middle High German drëschen, from Old High German drëskan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną. Compare Low German dörschen, Dutch dorsen, English thresh, Danish tærske.

verb:drehen.tx: From Middle High German dræjen, dræhen, from Old High German drāen (akin to Old Saxon thrāian), from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną. Cognate with Bavarian drahn, Dutch draaien and English throw.

noun:Daumen.tx: From Middle High German dūme, from Old High German dūmo. Compare German Low German Dumen, Dutch duim, English thumb, Danish tomme, Swedish tumme.

noun:Dichtung.tx: dichten + -ung, with the "poetry" sense invoking the "to compose" sense, and the "seal" sense the "to caulk, seal" sense.

adv:damals.tx: From da + Mal + -s. Compare Yiddish דעמאָלט (demolt) and דעמאָלטס (demolts).

noun:Dohle.tx: From Middle High German tole, tāle, tāhele (diminutive of tāhe), from Old High German tāhala, diminutive of tāha. The modern form is not inherited from written Middle High German but is a Central German dialect form (with unshifted d- and dialectal -ā- → -ō-).

noun:Damm.tx: From Middle High German tamm. Probably via Old High German *tamm from Proto-West Germanic *damm, from Proto-Germanic *dammaz, though it is sometimes considered a later back-formation from the verb dämmen. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dam).

noun:Dampf.tx: From Middle High German dampf, tampf, from Old High German thamph, damph, tamph, from Proto-Germanic *dampaz. Given the predominant d- in Old High German and quite frequent attestations with th- in related words, the underlying form in High German is probably *þampaz; also attested in the Old Saxon verb thempian. The origin of this byform seems unclear. Eventually derived from Proto-Germanic …

noun:Darm.tx: From Middle High German darm, from Old High German darm, from Proto-West Germanic *þarm, from Proto-Germanic *þarmaz. Cognate with Old Norse þarmr (whence Danish tarm), obsolete English tharms (“twisted guts”). Compare Ancient Greek τόρμος (tórmos, “hole”).

noun:Dattel.tx: From Middle High German datel, dactel, from Old High German dahtil, from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, literally “finger”), a folk-etymological alteration of a Semitic word; compare Hebrew דֶּקֶל (deqel). First attested in the 11th century CE form dahtilboum (“date tree”).

verb:dauern.tx: From Middle High German dūren, borrowed from Middle Low German dūren, itself from Latin dūrō. Compare Dutch duren, English dure.

noun:Degen.tx: Since ca. 1400, at first as degen, but also dege, dägen, tägen. Usually derived from Middle French dague, but the origin of the e-vocalism is unclear. An eastern dialectal *degue is possible, but apparently unattested, whereas Czech dýka is considered a borrowing from German. See French dague and Italian daga for more. Probably also related with the family of English dagger. From the 17th …

noun:Deich.tx: From Middle Low German dīk, from Old Saxon dīk, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz. Originally the same word as Teich (“pond”). The sense “dike” spread via Low German, for which reason the form Deich is most often regarded as an artificial adaptation of Middle Low German dīk (“dike”) to the phonetic system of standard German. However, Deich is also the form natively …

noun:Deichsel.tx: From Middle High German dīhsel, from Old High German dīhsala, from Proto-West Germanic *þīhslu, from Proto-Germanic *þinhslō.

noun:Delle.tx: From Middle High German telle, from Old High German *tella, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *daljō. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German delle). The form Tell(e) persists dialectally. Cognate with Dutch (dialectal) del and English dell.

noun:Demut.tx: From Middle High German dēmuot, diemuot, diemüete, from southern Old High German thiomuotī (ca. 800), from thio (“unfree, adscript”) + muot (“mood, attitude”), thus literally “serf-mindedness”. The word spread from Upper German during Middle High German times, gradually displacing the northern ōtmuotī (compare Old Saxon ōthmōdī). Northern sources almost invariably show -e- instead of -ie-, but …

noun:Diele.tx: From Middle High German dille, from Old High German dilla, from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ. More at thill. The sense “hallway” is from Middle Low German dēle and its German Low German descendants. The form, Diele, likewise seems influenced by Low German (although it could stem from an attested Middle High German variant dile). Cognate with Dutch deel f.

noun:Dienst.tx: From Middle High German dienst, dienest, from Old High German dionest, dionōst, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz. Compare the Old English þēonest, þēnest. See also German dienen.

noun:Dirne.tx: From Middle High German dierne (“girl; servant”), from Old High German diorna, thiorna (“girl; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *þewernā. Doublet of Deern. The sense “prostitute” developed from the use for a “girl from the lower classes”. It is first attested in the 15th century.

noun:Docht.tx: From Middle High German tāht, from Old High German tāht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtu-/*þæhta- (“thread”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to weave”). Cognate with Old Norse þáttr, for which reason the onset t- is an irregular hardening (compare tausend). The modern form is not inherited from literary Middle High German, but from the vernaculars. It has d- due to dialectal High German, …

noun:Dorsch.tx: From Middle High German dorsch, borrowed from Middle Low German dorsch, itself from Old Norse þorskr, from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz.

noun:Dotter.tx: From Middle High German toter, tuter, from Old High German totoro, tutaro, from Proto-West Germanic *dodrō. The modern form with initial d- and internal -tt- is of dialectal, probably Bavarian, origin.

noun:Drang.tx: Akin to the verb dringen (“to press”). From Proto-Germanic *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”). Cognate with English throng and Dutch drang.

verb:dringen.tx: From Middle High German dringen, from Old High German dringan. Akin to drängen and Drang. Cognate with dialectal English thring and, more distantly, with English throng.

noun:Duft.tx: From Middle High German tuft, from Old High German duft, thuft, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”) (DWDS); cognate with Danish duft (“fragrance”) and possibly Ancient Greek τῠφλός (tŭphlós, “blind”). The Middle High German t- is an irregular hardening (compare tausend) that was undone in modern German.

noun:Dunst.tx: From Middle High German dunst, tunst, from Old High German tunst, from Proto-Germanic *dunstą (“haze, mist, dust, evaporation”). Related to English dust. The onset d- is already predominant in Middle High German, thus due to irregular re-voicing. The expected form tunst disappears in early modern German under the reinforcing influence of Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dūst, from Old Saxon thunst).

noun:Drohne.tx: Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German drōne (variant of commoner drāne), from Old Saxon drāna, from Proto-West Germanic *drānu, from Proto-Germanic *drēnuz. The Low German form replaced older Tren(e), Trän(e), from Middle High German trën(e), from Old High German trëno, from the Germanic ablaut variant *drenô. This may have been reinforced by the desire to avoid homonymy with Träne (“tear”). The word …

noun:Dunkel.tx: From Middle High German tunkel, from Old High German tunkalī.

adv:drinnen.tx: From dr- + innen; the first component is from a short form of dar-.

adv:draußen.tx: From dr- + außen; the first component is from a short form of dar-.

noun:Dicke.tx: From Middle High German dicke, from Old High German dicchī; analysable as dick + -e.

adj:dicht.tx: From Middle High German dīchte, from Old High German dīhti, from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German dicht(e) with Low German shortening before -cht (compare German leicht and German Low German licht). The expected form deicht is attested in early modern German. Cognate with Dutch dicht, English tight.

adv:dicht.tx: From Middle High German dīchte, from Old High German dīhti, from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German dicht(e) with Low German shortening before -cht (compare German leicht and German Low German licht). The expected form deicht is attested in early modern German. Cognate with Dutch dicht, English tight.

verb:deuten.tx: From Middle High German diuten, from Old High German diuten, from Proto-West Germanic *þiudijan, from Proto-Germanic *þiudijaną, derived from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”), whence also comes Old English þēod (“people, nation”). Cognate with Dutch duiden, Icelandic þýða (“translate”), Swedish tyda, Danish tyde.

adj:derb.tx: From a Low German merger of two unrelated adjectives: (1.) Old Saxon therbi (“unleavened”), from Proto-Germanic *þerbaz; and (2.) Old Saxon derbi (“coarse, warlike”). Both regularly collapsed in Middle Low German derve (“firm, bold”). Older High German had only the former of the two adjectives and lacked the other: Middle High German derp (“unleavened”), from Old High German derb (“unleavened”). …

adv:derb.tx: From a Low German merger of two unrelated adjectives: (1.) Old Saxon therbi (“unleavened”), from Proto-Germanic *þerbaz; and (2.) Old Saxon derbi (“coarse, warlike”). Both regularly collapsed in Middle Low German derve (“firm, bold”). Older High German had only the former of the two adjectives and lacked the other: Middle High German derp (“unleavened”), from Old High German derb (“unleavened”). …

verb:dehnen.tx: From Middle High German denen, dennen, from Old High German thenen, thennen, from Proto-West Germanic *þannjan, from Proto-Germanic *þanjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch”). The simple -n- was generalised from certain inflected forms of the West Germanic verb. Cognate with Gothic 𐌿𐍆𐌸𐌰𐌽𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ufþanjan), Latin tenēre.

verb:dichten.tx: From Middle High German tihten, from Old High German tihtōn, dihtōn, Proto-West Germanic *dihtōn. The consonantism (d-/t-) was very unstable in early modern German; the voiced onset, which is in line with Middle Low German dichten, has prevailed. Cognate with Dutch dichten, English dight.

verb:drücken.tx: From Middle High German drücken, from Old High German drucchen, from Proto-West Germanic *þrukkijan. Doublet of drucken (“to print”), which was originally a southern variant, later standardized in a specialized sense.

verb:drängen.tx: From Middle High German drengen, from Old High German drengen, from Proto-West Germanic *þrangwijan, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat, press”). Absorbed related and roughly synonymous drangen (now obsolete), from Middle High German drangen, from Old High German drangōn, from Proto-West Germanic *þrang(w)ōn. This probably explains the ⟨ä⟩-spelling (cf. …

verb:drohen.tx: From Middle High German drōn, from Old High German drouwen; see dräuen (“to threaten”).

adj:dürr.tx: From Middle High German dürre, from Old High German durri, from Proto-West Germanic *þurʀī.

adj:düster.tx: From Middle Low German dûster, from Old Saxon thiustri, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *þiustrī (“dark, without light”). The word also exists in parts of West Central German (compare Luxembourgish däischter), which probably facilitated the borrowing; but the standardised form is definitely from Low German in view of its lacking diphthongisation.

adv:deshalb.tx: From Middle High German deshalp, from Middle High German des, dez (“from that, therefore, thereon”) + halp (“half”). Cognate to Low German diäßhalw (Paderbornisch).

noun:Dusche.tx: From French douche, from Italian doccia. The word became much more common after World War II, as the native word Brausebad had developed bad connotations.

verb:durchfahren.tx: From Middle High German durchvarn, from Old High German duruhfaran, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhfaran. Equivalent to durch- + fahren. Cognate with Dutch doorvaren and Old English þurhfaran.

adj:dermal.tx: From Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin”) + -al, possible influenced by English dermal.

verb:dingen.tx: From Middle High German dingen, from Old High German dingōn, from Proto-West Germanic *þingōn (“to hold a meeting”), from Proto-Germanic *þingōną. Originally a weak verb, which developed secondary strong forms; a process that seems to have begun in the Middle Low German cognate. Compare Dutch dingen (strong).

adj:drollig.tx: Via German Low German from early modern Dutch drollig.

noun:Dutzend.tx: From Middle High German tozen via tutzet, dutzet. Derived from Old French dozaine (today douzaine), from doze, from Latin duodecim. Not related to Dutch duizend (“thousand”).

conj:desto.tx: From Middle High German deste, from Old High German deste, theste, a contraction of des diu, respectively the genitive and instrumental case forms of Old High German daz n (“the; that, it”) respectively. Compare Dutch des te and English the ... the. Etymologically equivalent to des + die. The form ending in -o was by analogy to other adverbs and pronouns ending in -o in use in chancellery …

noun:Delphin.tx: From Middle High German delfīn, telfīn (13th c.), from Latin delphinus. Forms with diphthongization (Delphein) are hardly attestable, meaning that it was not fully integrated before the Modern German period.

phrase:den Ast absägen, auf dem man sitz.tx: Literally, “to saw off the branch on which one is sitting”.

noun:Drilling.tx: From Middle High German, related to drei (“three”), formed on the pattern of Zwilling (“pair, twin”).

noun:Drachen.tx: Alternative form of Drache (“dragon”), secondarily specified to two (among each other unrelated) special meanings of the word.

noun:Diskussion.tx: Borrowed from Latin discussiō, derived from the verb discutere.

noun:Dschungel.tx: Borrowed from English jungle, ultimately from Sanskrit जङ्गल (jaṅgala).

noun:Düne.tx: Via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch dûne, from Old Dutch dūna, from Proto-Germanic *dūnǭ. Middle Dutch origin is assured by the German -ü- (compare Süden). The more common Middle Low German form was dûne (with a back vowel -u-); this form may be originally Low German or an earlier borrowing from Dutch. Compare modern Dutch duin.

noun:Draisine.tx: From Drais + -ine. Named after Baron Karl Drais (1785–1851).

noun:Dekade.tx: Borrowed from French décade (“period of ten days or years”), from Latin decas, from Ancient Greek δεκάς (dekás). In contemporary French décennie is standard for “ten years, decade”.

adj:diplomatisch.tx: First attested in the 18th century. By surface analysis, Diplom + -at- + -isch.

noun:Diebstahl.tx: From Middle High German diupstāle, compound of diep (“thief”) (modern Dieb) and stāle, deverbal noun from stëln (“to steal”) (modern stehlen), from Old High German stëlan.

noun:Dynastie.tx: 16th century, from Latin dynastīa, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía). Usual since the 18th century, probably reinforced by French dynastie.

adj:durchsichtig.tx: From Middle High German durchsihtec, from Old High German duruhsihtīg, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhsihtīg. By surface analysis, Durchsicht + -ig. Cognate with Dutch doorzichtig.

noun:Detektiv.tx: 19th century, from English detective. The pronunciation with a second [d] may be due to simple assimilation, but it is also conceivable that the detek-sequence was popularly associated with entdecken (“to discover”). Note that the same pronunciation is also heard for Dutch detective in Belgium.

noun:Daumenregel.tx: Calque of English rule of thumb, Daumen + Regel.

noun:Demagogie.tx: From Latin dēmagōgia, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγίᾱ (dēmagōgíā).

noun:Datei.tx: Daten (“data”) + -ei, after Kartei (“card index, card catalogue”).

noun:Doktor.tx: Borrowed from Latin doctor, from docēre.

noun:Desertation.tx: From desertieren + -ation, formed by wrong analogy with other Latinate verbs in -ieren which form a corresponding noun in -ation, such as deklinieren (from Latin declinare) → Deklination (from Latin declinatio), and possibly in part by confusion with the similar-sounding Dissertation. The proper Latinate form is Desertion.

noun:Despotismus.tx: Borrowed from Latin despotismus. By surface analysis, Despot (“despot”) + -ismus.

noun:Defizit.tx: From French déficit, from Latin dēficit.

noun:Durchschnitt.tx: Deverbal from durchschneiden, equivalent to durch- + Schnitt.

noun:Durchbruch.tx: From durchbrechen; equivalent to durch + Bruch.

noun:Dürre.tx: From Middle High German dürre, from Old High German durrī, from Proto-West Germanic *þurʀī, from Proto-Germanic *þursuz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ters-. Equivalent to dürr (“dry”) + -e (“-ness”).

noun:Diät.tx: Borrowed from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita).

noun:Diagramm.tx: From French diagramme, from Italian diagramma, from Ancient Greek διάγραμμα (diágramma).

noun:Drainage.tx: From French drainage, from English drainage.

noun:Dinkel.tx: From Middle High German dinkel, from Old High German dinchel, further origin unknown.

noun:Dietrich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German Dietrich, from Old High German Diotrih, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Þeudōrīks. By surface analysis, Diet + -rich.

noun:Dämon.tx: Borrowed from Latin daemōn, borrowed from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn).

adv:dalli.tx: Borrowed from Polish dalej (“come on!, forward!”, literally “further”).

adj:desaströs.tx: Borrowed from French désastreux. Equivalent to Desaster + -ös.

noun:Dreitagebart.tx: From drei + Tage + Bart, literally “three-days beard”.

noun:Dialekt.tx: Borrowed from Latin dialectos f, from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος f (diálektos).

noun:Derivat.tx: From Latin dērīvātum. By surface analysis, derivieren + -at.

noun:Dekret.tx: From Middle High German decrēt, from Latin dēcrētum.

adj:delikat.tx: Borrowed from French délicat, from Latin dēlicātus.

adj:diskret.tx: From French discret, from Latin discretus.

noun:Depp.tx: Originally Upper German. Related to täppisch (“clumsy”) from Tappe (“paw”).

noun:Dünnbrettbohrer.tx: dünn (“slim”) + Brett (“plank”) + Bohrer (“driller”), originally in the context of craftsmanship or home improvement, someone who prefers easy tasks, drilling only slim boards/planks and leaving the more difficult thicker ones for others (or for later).

noun:Dosenöffner.tx: From Dose (“can, tin, box”, vulgarly “vulva”) + -n- + Öffner (“opener”).

noun:Dübel.tx: From Middle High German tübel, from Old High German tubil, from Proto-Germanic *dubilaz, probably derived from *dubjaną (whence English to dub). The modern onset d- is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dövel and see the obsolete variant above). Cognate with Dutch deuvel, perhaps also English dowel (see there).

noun:Depesche.tx: From Middle French depesche (Modern French dépêche).

noun:Dreikönigsfest.tx: From drei + König + -s- + Fest. Literally, “three kings' festival”.

verb:donnern.tx: From Middle High German donern, from Old High German thonarōn, synchronically analyzed as Donner (“thunder”) + -n (“verbal suffix”).

noun:Däne.tx: Inherited from Middle High German Tene, from Old High German *Teni, from Proto-Germanic *daniz. The modern D- is Central and Low German (Middle Low German Dēne), reinforced by Danish dansk, Danmark. These latter probably also caused the ä-spelling.

adv:deswegen.tx: Univerbation of des (“the, that”) + wegen (“because of”), using postpositive wegen.

adj:dreist.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German drîste, from Old Saxon thrīsti, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīstī.

adv:demnach.tx: Univerbation of dem + nach (“following, according to”) in postpositional use.

adv:daher.tx: Inherited from Middle High German dâ her, from Old High German dâr hera. By surface analysis, da + her.

noun:Desaster.tx: Ca. 1800, from French désastre, itself from Italian disastro. The now predominant pronunciation with a long vowel is unusual; English influence would be a plausible but speculative explanation.

noun:Dresdner.tx: Dresden + -er, with syncope of the middle e.

adj:Dresdner.tx: Dresden + -er, with syncope of the middle e.

noun:Dokument.tx: From Latin documentum. First attested in the 16th century.

noun:Diva.tx: From Italian diva, from Latin divus 'divinity'.

noun:Drehleier.tx: From drehen (“to turn”) + Leier (“lyre”). Compare Dutch draailier.

noun:Denkfabrik.tx: From denken (“to think”) + Fabrik (“factory”), perhaps a calque of English think factory.

noun:Dinosaurier.tx: From Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “fearful, mighty”) and σαῦρος (saûros), in Herodot a varia lectio of σαύρα (saúra), Ionic σαύρη (saúrē, “lizard”).

adv:darauf.tx: From Middle High German dar uf, equivalent to dar- (“there”) + auf (“up”) (or dar + auf). Compare English thereupon.

verb:dramatisieren.tx: From the stem of Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma) + -isieren. First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Dosis.tx: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), from Proto-Hellenic *dótis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis.

noun:Digestif.tx: From French digestif, from Latin dīgestīvus. Doublet of digestiv.

verb:duzen.tx: From Middle High German duzen, dutzen, dützen, from Old High German *dūzzen, *dūezzen, equivalent to du + -zen. Compare Middle English thouten.

noun:Drahtzieher.tx: From Draht (“wire”) + ziehen (“to pull”) + -er, literally “wire puller”.

noun:Duplikat.tx: Borrowed from Latin duplicātum, the substantivized neuter singular of duplicātus (perfect passive participle of duplicō). Cognate with French duplicatum. By surface analysis, duplizieren + -at.

noun:Drückeberger.tx: 19th century. From (sich) drücken (“to shirk”) + Berger, as if being the demonym of an imaginary town Drückeberg (literally “shirk mountain”).

adj:deutlich.tx: From Middle High German diuticlīche (adverb), equivalent to deuten + -lich.

adv:deutlich.tx: From Middle High German diuticlīche (adverb), equivalent to deuten + -lich.

noun:Domäne.tx: Borrowed from French domaine, 16th century. Doublet of Domain.

verb:dekorieren.tx: From French décorer + -ieren from Latin decorō.

noun:Düker.tx: Formally from Low German Düker, from Middle Low German düker (“diver”, also “culvert”?). Doublet of Taucher ("diver"). The sense “culvert” may be a loan translation of Dutch duiker. At least its adoption into standard German was probably reinforced by Dutch.

adj:dämlich.tx: Borrowed from German Low German form that in standard usage replaced High German dämisch, damisch from the same source. Various theories about the etymology have been suggested: * It may be cognate with Latin tēmētum. * It may be related to taumeln (“to tumble”), but this is unlikely since forms with t- are not attested. * It may be related to dämmern (“to become dim”), but this is also rejected …

verb:düngen.tx: From Middle High German tüngen, from Old High German -tungen (in gitungen), derived from tung (“dung”). The modern consontanism is formally Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German düngen), but it must be due largely to dialectal re-voicing given that Dung (which see for more) was a predominantly southern word.

noun:Downsyndrom.tx: From English Down + Syndrom, named after English physician John Langdon Haydon Down (1828–1896).

verb:demolieren.tx: From Latin dēmōlīrī, with influence from French démolir.

verb:drillen.tx: Seemingly from Middle Low German and/or Middle Dutch drillen, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *þurhil (“perforated, hole”). The verb may have existed in Middle High German, but only a strong past participle gedrollen (“round”) is attested. The Upper German dialects have a verb trillen, which is probably a variant of drillen (compare Dutch drillen and trillen; English thrill and trill).

adv:derzeit.tx: Univerbation of der + Zeit, a temporal genitive. Compare the identical Dutch destijds.

verb:dünken.tx: From Middle High German dunken, from Old High German dunken, from Proto-West Germanic *þunkijan, from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną.

adv:daheim.tx: From Middle High German dāheim, dāheime, darheime, from Old High German dārheime (“at home”), equivalent to da + heim. Compare Middle High German heime (“home, at home”, adverb), Old High German heime, heimi (“home, at home”, adverb), Bavarian dahoam.

noun:Dornröschen.tx: From Dorn (“thorn”) + Rose (“rose”) + -chen (diminutive suffix), cognate to Dutch Doornroosje. Compare English Little Briar Rose, an alternate name for Sleeping Beauty (the tale and the character).

verb:destillieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin dēstīllō (“to trickle down”).

adj:defensiv.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin defensivus, from Latin dēfendō.

adv:darüber.tx: dar- + über, from Middle High German dār über, from Old High German dâr dara ubari. Compare English thereover.

adv:dafür.tx: From Middle High German dāvür, dārvür, from Old High German dār furi, dāra furi; equivalent to da + für. Compare English therefore.

adv:daran.tx: From Middle High German dāran, dārane, from Old High German dār ana, dāra ana (“thereon, on or at that (place)”). See da, an. More at thereon.

adv:dabei.tx: da + bei. Compare English thereby, Yiddish דערבײַ (derbay).

adv:darum.tx: Middle High German darumme, dar umme, darumbe, dar umbe, from Old High German dār (“there”) umbi (“around”). By surface analysis, dar- + um.

adv:drüben.tx: From dr- + üben, with üben a rare word formed from über in analogy to pairs like unter - unten, ober - oben.

adj:derangiert.tx: Inflected form of the dated derangieren, from French déranger.

pt: there; from there, out of there, thence
adv:daraus.tx: From Middle High German darūz, from Old High German darūz, daraūz (“out of that; out of there”), equivalent to dar- (“there; from there, out of there, thence”) + aus (“out”). Compare archaic English thereout.

noun:Deklaration.tx: From Latin dēclārātiō. See English declaration.

noun:Diözese.tx: From Ecclesiastical Latin dioecesis, from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis).

noun:Dekan.tx: 15th century, from Medieval Latin decānus. Doublet of Dechant.

noun:Dickicht.tx: Formed from dick (“thick”), similar to Old English þiccet.

adj:demütig.tx: From Middle High German diemüetec, from Old High German diomuotīg, from Old High German dio (“servant”) + *muotīg (“minded”), equivalent to Demut (“humility”) + -ig.

adv:danach.tx: From Middle High German danāch, darnāch, from Old High German daranāh, equivalent to da (“there”) + nach (“after”). Compare Yiddish דערנאָך (dernokh).

adv:dadurch.tx: From Middle High German dadurch, dādurch, from Old High German dārduruh. Equivalent to da- + durch.

noun:Demonstrant.tx: From Latin dēmōnstrāns. First attested in the second half of the 18th century.

noun:Drittel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German dritteil n; compare dritte + Teil.

verb:dämpfen.tx: From Middle High German dempfen, Old High German dempfen, from Proto-Germanic *dampijaną (“to dampen, make damp”).

noun:Diskriminierung.tx: diskriminieren + -ung, possibly after French discrimination, use in German from the 1920s.

noun:Dienstreise.tx: From Dienst (“service, dutiful (e.g. professional) action”) + Reise (“voyage, journey”).

noun:Dämmerung.tx: From Middle High German demerunge, from Old High German demerunga, extended form of demar. The spelling with -ä- is unetymological.

noun:Deckel.tx: From Middle High German deckel, equivalent to decken + -el. Cognate with Middle Low German deckel (“lid, covering”).

adj:drall.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German dral. Pertains to drillen (“to tighten”) and drehen (“to turn”).

adj:deftig.tx: Via German Low German from Dutch deftig, itself seemingly from West Frisian. The original sense of the Dutch word is not quite clear but would have run on the lines of “suitable, solid, weighty”. The further semantic development has been such that the word now, arguably, has opposite senses in German (“coarse, rustic”) and Dutch (“refined, genteel”).

verb:durchschauen.tx: From Middle High German durchschouwen, from Old High German duruhskouwōn. Equivalent to durch- + schauen.

noun:Dünung.tx: Borrowed from Low German Dünung, from dunen (“to expand”), probably related to Dumen (“thumb”), for which see Old Saxon thūmo.

adj:diesig.tx: From German Low German. Pertains to Middle Low German disinge (“hazy weather”). Compare Dutch (regional) dijzig.

noun:Diakon.tx: From Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos).

verb:dunkeln.tx: From Middle High German dunkeln, tunkeln, from Old High German tunkalēn, tunkalen. By surface analysis, dunkel + -n.

verb:ducken.tx: From Middle High German tucken, tücken. Pertains to tauchen (“to dive”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German ducken). Related to English duck.

pron:dergleichen.tx: From der (genitive plural) + gleich (“like, alike”) + -en. Compare Dutch dergelijk.

adj:dreißigste.tx: From Middle High German drīzigeste, drīzegeste, from Old High German drīzugōsto, equivalent to dreißig + -ste.

verb:driften.tx: 20th century, from Drift + -en. Doublet of triften.

verb:draufgehen.tx: From drauf- + gehen, literally “to go on it”.

adv:dannen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German dannen, from Old High German danana, from Proto-West Germanic *þananā, extension of *þan. Cognates include Bavarian dauna, daune, dauni and English thence.

noun:Dusel.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German. Related to dösen (“to doze”).

verb:dösen.tx: From German Low German dösen, from Middle High German dōsen (“to snooze, slumber" also "to roar, rustle, whizz, snore”), from Old High German dōsōn (“to roar”), from Proto-West Germanic *þus- (“to roar”), related to Middle High German dœsen, tœsen (“to scatter, destroy”); ultimately from the root of Dunst (“haze”). Compare dösig for more.

noun:Drachenfutter.tx: From Drache (“dragon”) + -n- + Futter (“fodder”). The sense of "placating gift" is from around 1900, building on the metaphor of dragons from Drachen in the sense of "cantankerous woman".

noun:Dost.tx: From Middle High German doste, from Old High German dost, dosto (“origanum; tuft”). Further origin unknown. According to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”), see also Norwegian tust (“tuft”), Proto-Germanic *þūmô (“thumb”). Compare Middle Low German doste (either cognate or from the High German).

noun:Donnerwetter.tx: From Donner (“thunder”) + Wetter (“weather”). First attested as donrewedder (Ripuarian, late 15th c.).

intj:Donnerwetter.tx: From Donner (“thunder”) + Wetter (“weather”). First attested as donrewedder (Ripuarian, late 15th c.).

noun:Dreikäsehoch.tx: Univerbation of drei + Käse + hoch, literally “three cheeses high/tall”. Compare French haut comme trois pommes and Czech trpaslík.

verb:dröhnen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German dronen, from Middle Low German drönen, from Old Saxon *drunnian, from Proto-West Germanic *drunnjan, from Proto-Germanic *drunjaną.

noun:Dudelsack.tx: Formally dudeln (“play monotone music, tootle”) + Sack (“sack, bag”). While it is uncertain whether the verb dudeln as such is originally Slavic or not, its use in Dudelsack is definitely based on Czech and/or Polish dudy (“bagpipes”). The latter was also borrowed into early modern German as Dudei.

noun:Dreifaltigkeit.tx: From Middle High German drīvaltecheit f, from drīvaltec (“triune”) + -heit, from drīvalt (“threefold”) + -eg, from Old High German thrī̌falt, from thrī (“three”) + -falt. Equivalent to dreifaltig + -keit.

verb:durchgehen.tx: From Middle High German durchgān, from Old High German duruhgān, thuruhgān, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhgān. Equivalent to durch- (“through”) + gehen (“to go”). Cognate with Dutch doorgaan, English go through and obsolete thoroughgo.

adj:durcheinander.tx: From Middle High German durcheinander, equivalent to durch- + einander. Cognate with Middle Low German dörchênander, German Low German dörnanner.

noun:Durian.tx: From English durian, from Malay durian, from Proto-Malayic *duri-an, from (Western) Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *duʀi-an.

noun:Dreckloch.tx: From Dreck (“dirt, filth, shit”) + Loch (“hole, pit”).

noun:Deutung.tx: From Middle High German diutunge. By surface analysis, deuten + -ung.

noun:Druse.tx: Borrowed from Arabic دُرُوز (durūz, dialectally drūz), plural of دُرْزِيّ (durziyy, “Druze”), named after الدَرَزِيّ (ad-daraziyy, “Ad-Darazi”), the Persian founder of the faith.

adv:diesmal.tx: Univerbation of dies Mal (“this time”), a variant of dieses Mal.

verb:darbringen.tx: From Middle High German darbringen, from Old High German tharabringan. By surface analysis, dar- + bringen.

noun:Durchschlag.tx: durch- + Schlag. Compare the noun Durchschlagen, nominalisation of the verb durchschlagen

adj:dumpf.tx: Gradation from Middle High German dimpfen (“to smoke, fume”), and related to Dampf (“steam”), see there for more. English dank has been speculated to be related.

noun:Dreh.tx: Deverbal from drehen, after Low German Dreih m (compare Dutch draai). Chiefly since the 19th century, earlier attestations are isolated. Widely displaced older Drehe f. The sense “trick” is from Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant).

noun:Detektion.tx: Borrowed from English detection, from Latin dētēctiōnem.

noun:Doppel.tx: Related to doppeln. Doublet of Zweifel.

noun:Doxologie.tx: From Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).

noun:Drink.tx: Borrowed from English drink. Doublet of Trunk. See also Trank.

adv:durchaus.tx: From Late Middle High German durch ūȥ (“entirely through, all the way”). Equivalent to durch (“through”) + aus (“out”). Compare English throughout and Yiddish דורכויס (durkhoys).

noun:Dissertation.tx: Borrowed from Latin dissertātiō, from dissertō.

verb:dünsten.tx: From Middle High German dunsten, dünsten. Grimm remarks on this verb and dunsten having historically been considered alternative forms without distinction, but already adds that the transitive sense is exclusive to the umlated form.

noun:Dezernat.tx: Borrowed from Latin dēcernat, third-person singular present active subjunctive of dēcernō (“to decide”).

noun:Delegierter.tx: Substantivization of delegiert (“delegated”); see delegieren (“to delegate”) for more.

adv:deinetwegen.tx: Shortened from von deinetwegen, which can be traced through two developmental routes. One route is from von deinentwegen / von deinent wegen, from von deinen wegen, from Middle High German von dînen wegen, in which wegen was the dative plural of modern-day Weg and dînen was the possessive pronoun in the dative plural. Another route can be traced from von deintwegen / von deint wegen, from Middle …

noun:Durchgang.tx: From Middle High German durchganc, from Old High German duruhgang, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhgang. By surface analysis, deverbal from durchgehen or durch + Gang.

noun:Driss.tx: From Central Franconian Dress (“excrement”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *dritą.

noun:Deut.tx: Borrowed from Dutch duit, a historic coin of minor value. Cognate to Danish døjt.

verb:durchkommen.tx: From Middle High German durchkomen, from Old High German duruhkweman, duruhqueman, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhkweman. Equivalent to durch- (“through”) + kommen (“to come”). Cognate with Dutch doorkomen.

phrase:das war's.tx: Literally, “that was it”. Compare Dutch dat was 'm.

verb:dümpeln.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German dümpelen. Probably related to Tümpel (“shallow pond”). Cognate with Dutch dompelen.

phrase:der Amtsschimmel wiehert.tx: From Amtsschimmel and wiehern. Literally, “the official service horse is whinnying”.

adj:dufte.tx: From Hebrew טוֹב (tov, “good”), via Yiddish and Rotwelsch. Compare Dutch tof.

verb:dampfen.tx: Verbal formation related to Dampf (“steam, vapor”).

noun:Dudu.tx: From the address du, du! (“you, you!”), said to a child in admonition.

verb:dämmen.tx: From Middle High German temmen, from Old High German -temmen in bitemmen, ultimately from the root of Damm (“embankment”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German as in Damm (compare Middle Low German demmen).

noun:Deibel.tx: Regional forms of Teufel (“devil”); in the case of Deibel: East Central German. These have spread supraregionally, possibly due to the fact that mentioning the devil’s name was considered obscene (for religious or superstitious reasons).

noun:Denkzettel.tx: denken + Zettel, literally “think note”. At first in Middle Low German denkcēdel (“judicial certificate”).

noun:Dez.tx: Borrowed from Low German. Further origin unknown. Speculations include a relation with French tête(s).

adj:dösig.tx: From German Low German dösig, from Middle Low German dȫsich, from Old Saxon *dosig, *dusig, from Proto-West Germanic *dusīg (“stunned, dazed, giddy”), cognate with English dizzy. The Low German and Middle Low German words mean only “dazed, dizzy, dumb/stupid”, so it is certain that the German word also comprehends new formation from related dösen (“to doze, daydream”) + -ig. Related also to …

noun:Drift.tx: Low German doublet of Trift (“path on which livestock is driven”). From Middle Low German drift, from Proto-West Germanic *drifti, from the verb *drīban, whence German treiben (“to drive”). Compare English drift.

adj:dröge.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German drȫge (“dry”), from Old Saxon *drōgi, from Proto-Germanic *draugiz. Also a Central German form; compare Ripuarian drüch, Luxembourgish dréchen (“dry”). Related to Upper German trocken and, in early modern German, used as a mere dialectal variant of it. In the contemporary sense reintroduced via German Low German (19th century). Cognate with dry and Dutch droog.

adj:dummdreist.tx: Borrowed from the Middle Low German compound dumdrīste, in which dum (dumm) did not mean "stupid" but rather "reckless". Later interpreted more literally as dumm + dreist, literally “dumb-brash”.

noun:Dussel.tx: A byform of Dusel (“dizziness”), borrowed from German Low German Dusel (“drowsiness; dizziness”), from Middle Low German dusen, dosen (“to sway; stagger; wander; be dizzy”). More at doze, dizzy.

noun:Dutt.tx: From German Low German. Further origin unknown.

noun:Display.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English display. The initial stress in German as a generalisation of the predominant English stress pattern (doubtless unrelated to the equivalent pronunciation in a small minority of American speakers).

noun:Diet.tx: From Middle High German diet, from Old High German diot, diota, from Proto-West Germanic *þeudu.

noun:Distelfink.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German distilfinco (also distilfogal). By surface analysis, Distel (“thistle”) + Fink (“finch”). Cognate with Dutch distelvink, English thistlefinch, and compare Latin carduelis, from carduus (“thistle”). Goldfinch favor thistle seeds as food, and use thistle down as nest material.

noun:Dozent.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin docēns, docentem (“teaching”).

adj:dornig.tx: From Middle High German dornec, from Old High German *dornig, *dornag, from Proto-West Germanic *þornag. Equivalent to Dorn + -ig.

noun:Dialektik.tx: Inherited from Middle High German dīalectike, from Latin dialecticē.

noun:Deern.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Deern. Doublet of Dirne (“girl; whore”).

noun:Dole.tx: Late Middle High German dol (“mine”), from Old High German dola (“pipe”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *dalą ~ *dalaz n or m (“valley”).

verb:durchlaufen.tx: From Middle High German durchloufen, from Old High German duruhloufan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhlaupan. Equivalent to durch + laufen. Cognate with Dutch doorlopen.

noun:Dieberei.tx: From Middle High German diuberīe, dīberīe, equivalent to Dieb + -erei. Cognate with German Low German Deveree, English thievery.

noun:Dickkopf.tx: Bahuvrīhi compound of dick (“thick, big”) + Kopf (“head”). Attested 16th c. in the literal sense.

noun:Draufgänger.tx: Formally equivalent to drauf (“on it”) + Gänger (“goer, one who goes”), after draufgehen (“to lead the charge, to go for it”).

verb:delegieren.tx: From Latin dēlēgāre. Compare English delegate, French déléguer, Danish delegere, Dutch delegeren.

phrase:die Hoffnung stirbt zuletzt.tx: Literally, “hope dies last”. Compare Italian la speranza è l'ultima a morire.

adj:dürftig.tx: From Middle High German dürftic, from Old High German durftic, ultimately from the root of dürfen (“to be allowed”).

noun:Durchreise.tx: From the verb durchreisen (“to travel through”).

noun:Dart.tx: Borrowed from English dart, from Old French dart, from Proto-West Germanic *darōþu.

adj:devot.tx: Borrowed from Latin devotus, from dēvoveō, from voveō.

adj:distinguiert.tx: Borrowed from French distingué, past participle of distinguer, from Latin distinguō.

adj:durchgängig.tx: From Middle High German durchgengic, from Old High German duruhgengīg. By surface analysis, durch + gängig or Durchgang + -ig.

adj:durchtrieben.tx: From Middle High German durchtrīben, equivalent to durch + treiben (“to drive”).

verb:durchbrechen.tx: From Middle High German durchbrechen, from Old High German duruhbrehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhbrekan; analyzable as durch (“through”) + brechen (“to break”).

noun:Drechsler.tx: From Middle High German dræhseler, from Old High German thrāhslāri; equivalent to drechseln (“to work a lathe”) + -er (“-er”).

noun:Dünkel.tx: 16th century, from Middle High German dunc (“thinking, point of view”) + -el. Probably coined by Luther. The Middle High German noun is deverbal from dünken (“to seem”).

phrase:da sei Gott vor.tx: Literally, “God be in front of it”, or more loosely translated as “may He block it from happening”. The splitting of the pronominal adverb davor suggests a northern or western German origin.

phrase:die Hütte brennt.tx: Literally, “the hut is on fire”. The phrase seems to have lexicalized in the late 1990s.

noun:Dummbatz.tx: From dumm + Batz. Compare to dumbass.

noun:Dilatation.tx: From Old French dilatation, from Late Latin dīlātātio.

phrase:da lachen ja die Hühner.tx: Literally, “the chickens (will) laugh at that”. Compare Russian курам на смех (kuram na smex, “for the chickens to laugh at”) with a similar meaning.

noun:Deadline.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English deadline. The feminine gender after Linie, Leine.

verb:durchlesen.tx: From Middle High German durchlësen, from Old High German duruhlësan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhlesan. Equivalent to durch- + lesen. Cognate with Dutch doorlezen.

phrase:das Kind fällt in den Brunnen.tx: Literally, “the child falls into the well”. From a now unused proverb where the farmer only sets out to cover his well when a child (or a calf, or the like) has already drowned in it.

verb:dudeln.tx: Either of imitative origin (lautmalend) or otherwise from the root of Dudelsack (“bagpipes”). Cognate with Polish dudlić (“to play the bagpipes”).

verb:durchschlagen.tx: From Middle High German durchslahen, from Old High German duruhslahan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhslahan. Equivalent to durch- + schlagen. Cognate with Dutch doorslaan.

noun:Dreistigkeit.tx: Derived from Middle Low German drīstichēt. Analyzable as dreist + -igkeit.

adj:doppelzüngig.tx: doppel- + Zunge + -ig, perhaps a calque of Latin bilinguis.

phrase:das Gelbe vom Ei.tx: Literally, “the yellow from the egg”, i.e. the yolk.

verb:durchsieben.tx: From durch + sieben (separable) or durch- + sieben (inseparable).

noun:Diech.tx: From Middle High German diech, from Old High German dioh, from Proto-Germanic *þeuhą. Cognate with Dutch dij, English thigh.

phrase:da liegt der Hase im Pfeffer.tx: Literally, “here the hare lies in the pepper”.

phrase:das Denken soll man den Pferden ü.tx: Literally, “one should leave the thinking to the horses”.

noun:Dornbusch.tx: Compound of Dorn (“thorn”) + Busch (“bush”). Cognate with Dutch doornbos, English thornbush and Swedish törnbuske, all meaning the same and having the same elements (stemming from Proto-Germanic *þurnaz + *buskaz), thus they either share a common Germanic root or are calques of this German term.

noun:Durchlaucht.tx: From Middle High German durchlūcht, a Central German byform of durchliuht(et), equivalent to modern durchleuchtet, literally “shone through”, thus “illuminated, shining”.

verb:durchleuchten.tx: From Middle High German durchliuhten, from Old High German duruhliuhten, duruhliohten. By surface analysis, durch- + leuchten.

verb:dürsten.tx: From Middle High German dürsten, dursten, from Old High German dursten, equivalent to Durst + -en.

verb:durchbohren.tx: From Middle High German durchborn, from Old High German duruhborōn. Equivalent to durch- + bohren.

noun:Dreispitz.tx: From drei + Spitz, calque of Latin tricornis.

noun:Daus.tx: From Middle High German dūs, from Old High German dūs, from Old French dous (“two”). Also sometimes applied to people, being most frequent in the old-fashioned interjection Ei der Daus (“"good grief", "well I never!", etc.”) (compare what the deuce), stemming from the deuce, the highest (or sometimes lowest) card being played, and hence having an ambiguously bold sense; however, descendants of …

noun:Deuter.tx: Inherited from Middle High German diutare, Old High German diutāri; equivalent to deuten + -er

pron:deinesgleichen.tx: deines (genitive case of personal pronoun 2 sg) + gleich (“similar, equal”)

adv:dazumal.tx: From Middle High German dō ze māle. Equivalent to a univerbation of da + zu + Mal.

verb:durchsehen.tx: From Middle High German durchsehen, from Old High German duruhsehan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhsehwan. Equivalent to durch- + sehen

noun:Dienstherr.tx: From Middle High German dienstherre. Analyzable as Dienst + Herr.

noun:Durchschuss.tx: durch + Schuss or deverbal from durchschießen.

noun:Dreifuß.tx: drei (“three”) + Fuß (“foot”); calque of Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous).

verb:drechseln.tx: From Middle High German dræhseln, dræhsel, from Old High German drāhsil; akin to drehen (“to turn”).

noun:Dagga.tx: Borrowed from Afrikaans dagga, from Khoekhoe daxab.

verb:doktern.tx: From Doktor + -n. Spelt with -er- after the popular pronunciation, reflected here by analogy with verbs in -ern (comparable to Google vs. googeln).

adv:dorten.tx: 16th century variant of dort. Compare Bavarian duatn.

verb:durchstehen.tx: From Middle High German *durchstēn, *durchstān, from Old High German duruhstēn, duruhstān, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhstān. Equivalent to durch- + stehen. Compare Dutch doorstaan.

verb:durchficken.tx: From durch + ficken, literally “to fuck through(out)”.

noun:Dolle.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German dolle, from Proto-Germanic *þullaz (“thole, rowlock”).

noun:Dornröschenschlaf.tx: Dornröschen + Schlaf (From the Brothers Grimm fairy tale Sleeping Beauty, in which a princess is cursed to sleep for a hundred years.)

noun:Discjockey.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English disc jockey

phrase:der Appetit kommt beim Essen.tx: Calque of French l'appétit vient en mangeant.

phrase:da beißt die Maus keinen Faden ab.tx: Literally, “the mouse won’t bite off a thread”. After the fable Le Lion et le Rat by Jean de La Fontaine.

verb:dekantieren.tx: Borrowed from French décanter + -ieren, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from Latin canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).

noun:Donnerbüchse.tx: Calque of Dutch donderbus, Donner + Büchse, literally “thunder gun”.

phrase:das Leben ist kein Ponyhof.tx: Playful adaptation of the older snowclone Das Leben ist kein X, where X is conventionally based on a verb. Compare Dutch het leven is geen ponykamp.

adv:druff.tx: From dr- + uff, see the latter.

noun:Dunstkreis.tx: Dunst + Kreis, calque of Latin atmosphaera.

adj:dahergelaufen.tx: Past participle of an unusual or southern daherlaufen with the sense of herbeilaufen (“to arrive”), vorbeilaufen (“to pass by”); thus “whoever happens to walk by”.

verb:degradieren.tx: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin dēgradāre, influenced by French dégrader, de- + gradieren.

noun:Dummerjan.tx: Univerbation of dummer + Jan, literally “stupid John” (16th century). The optionally lengthened vowel as well as the byform above are due to influence of Grobian, Schlendrian (of different formation).

noun:Dinner.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English dinner. Doublet of Diner.

adv:dermaßen.tx: Univerbation of der + Maßen, literally "of that measure, of that degree", using a genitive construction with now largely obsolete feminine gender of Maß. Compare also einigermaßen, folgendermaßen for similar constructions. Cognate with Dutch dermate.

noun:Debitkarte.tx: From English debit or French débit + Karte, a partial calque of English debit card.

verb:durchwursteln.tx: Probably from durch- (“through”) + Middle Low German worsteln (“to struggle”) (cognate with English to wrestle and Dutch worstelen), influenced by wursteln (“to tamper”, literally “to make sausages”).

verb:durchschneiden.tx: From Middle High German durchsnīden. By surface analysis, durch- + schneiden.

verb:durchstechen.tx: From Middle High German durchstechen, from Old High German duruhstehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhstekan. Equivalent to durch- + stechen. Cognate with Dutch doorsteken.

noun:Dschunke.tx: From Italian giunco / giunca, from Portuguese junco, from Arabic جُنْك (junk), from Malay jong, from Javanese ꦗꦺꦴꦁ (jong), from Old Javanese joṅ (“seagoing ship”), probably ultimately from Proto-Mon-Khmer *d₂luuŋ ~ *d₂luŋ ~ *d₂luəŋ ~ *d₂ləŋ (“boat”). Compare English junk, Dutch jonk, French jonque, Spanish junco.

noun:Dechsel.tx: From Middle High German dehsele, from Old High German dehsala, thehsala, from Proto-West Germanic *þehsulā, from Proto-Germanic *þehsulǭ (“axe”). Cognate with Dutch dissel, Old Norse þexla.

noun:Diwan.tx: Borrowed from French divan, from Persian دیوان (divân).

noun:Direktrice.tx: Borrowed from French directrice. First attested in the 18th century.

verb:durchscheinen.tx: From Middle High German durchschīnen, from Old High German duruhskīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhskīnan. By surface analysis, durch- + scheinen. Cognate with Dutch doorschijnen.

noun:Dorade.tx: From French dorade, from Spanish dorada (“gilded one”); compare the German name.

phrase:die Katze beißt sich in den Schwa.tx: Literally, “the cat is biting its own tail”. Compare French c'est le chat qui se mord la queue and so on.

verb:doubeln.tx: From Double + -n. In the verb, the /əl/ syllable must be respelt phonetically; compare googeln from Google.

adv:drumherum.tx: From drum + herum, literally “around it around”.

noun:Dechant.tx: From Middle High German dechant, techant, from Old High German tehhant, tehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *dekan (“deacon”), from Latin decanus (“dean”). Doublet of Dekan, a 15th-century borrowing. In Middle Low German dēken, the full vowel in the second syllable was protected by adaptation to various Latin suffixes. The initial d- was also restored by relatinisation; compare already Old High …

verb:daddeln.tx: 20th century, from Low German daddeln, also dadeln, tateln (“to stutter, gabble, cackle”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare archaic German dadern, Dutch tateren, tatelen, English tattle. Originally said of the choppy sounds of slot machines.

verb:durchbringen.tx: From Middle High German durchbringen, from Old High German duruhbringan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhbringan. Equivalent to durch- + bringen.

noun:Disponent.tx: Borrowed from Latin dispōnēns (“disposing, distributing, arranging”) (genitive singular dispōnentis).

noun:Durchfahrt.tx: From durchfahren, by surface analysis, durch- + Fahrt.

phrase:da nicht für.tx: Literally, “there not for”, or more loosely translated as “there's nothing (to be thankful) for”. See also Russian не́ за что (né za što).

verb:demaskieren.tx: From French démasquer + -ieren. By surface analysis, de- + Maske + -ieren or de- + maskieren.

noun:Dämlack.tx: 19th century, derived from dämlich. The second syllable has been compared to Lackel (“yokel”), but this word is southwestern, whereas Dämlack appears to be of northeastern, especially Berlinian, origin. Therefore a derivation with the Slavic suffix *-akъ is more likely. Said suffix has been productive in various eastern German dialects.

verb:dezimieren.tx: Latin decimāre (“to take or offer a tenth part”)

noun:Durchreisender.tx: From durchreisend (“traveling through”) + -er; nominalization of the adjective durchreisend.

intj:denkste.tx: From denkst + -e. The idiomatic sense is an ellipsis of a phrase such as das denkste wohl / vielleicht (“that's what you may think”).

verb:durchgraben.tx: From Middle High German durchgraben, from Old High German duruhgraban, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhgraban. Equivalent to durch- + graben. Cognate with Dutch doorgraven.

phrase:das kommt davon.tx: Ellipsis of das kommt davon, wenn (man/du) .... Literally, “this comes from it”.

phrase:der Herzen.tx: Literally, “of the hearts [of the public]”. Generalized from Meister der Herzen (“champions of the hearts”), an epithet widely used by the media in 2001 referring to Schalke 04 after they had dramatically lost (in stoppage time of the last match) what would have been their first German championship since 1958.

pt: dialling; part of a phone number
noun:Durchwahl.tx: From durch (“through”) + Wahl (“dialling; part of a phone number”, literally “choice”).

verb:durchbeißen.tx: From Middle High German durchbīzen, from Old High German duruhbīzan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhbītan. Equivalent to durch- + beißen. Cognate with Dutch doorbijten and West Frisian trochbite.

verb:durchfließen.tx: From Middle High German durchvliezen, from Old High German duruhfliozan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhfleutan. Equivalent to durch- + fließen. Cognate with Dutch doorvlieten.

verb:durchfragen.tx: From durch- + fragen. Formally corresponding to Old High German duruhfrāgēn.

verb:durchleiten.tx: From Middle High German *durchleiten, from Old High German duruhleiten, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhlaidijan. Equivalent to durch- + leiten. Cognate with Dutch doorleiden.

verb:durchmischen.tx: From Middle High German durchmischen, from Old High German duruhmiskan. Equivalent to durch- + mischen.

noun:Damast.tx: Ca. 1400, from Italian damasto, older byform of damasco, from Damasco (“Damascus”).

noun:Durchführungsverordnung.tx: From Durchführung (“implementation; execution”) + -s- + Verordnung (“directive, decree; ordinance”).

noun:Doof.tx: See doof. The noun is from Central Franconian dialects, especially Ripuarian ones, in which nominalized masculine adjectives are endingless, e.g. dä Aal (“the old man”), dä Kleen (“the little one”). This continues Middle High German -e, which was apocopated; in attributive position this form was then replaced with the accusative in -e(n), whereas in nominalization it was generalized to all cases. …

noun:Dickhäuter.tx: Calque of New Latin Pachydermata, dick (“thick”) + Haut (“skin”) + -er.

phrase:das sind doch bürgerliche Kategor.tx: Literally, “But those are bourgeois categories.” Coined by German songwriter, cabaret artist and author Marc-Uwe Kling in 2009 for his book series The Kangaroo Chronicles.

noun:Demission.tx: 17th century, from Latin dimissio, chiefly through French démission.

noun:Dixi-Klo.tx: From DIXI, a trademarked brand of portable toilets in Germany, + Klo.

noun:Datenzentrum.tx: Daten + Zentrum, calque of English data centre.

noun:Direx.tx: Latinizing short form of Direktor, possibly in analogy with Latin rēx (“king”).

noun:Dissonanz.tx: Middle High German dissonantz, from Late Latin dissonantia.

phrase:das sagt der Richtige.tx: Literally, “you're the right one to say that”.

noun:Dulli.tx: Sense 1 and 2 are derived from the Low German adjective dull (“dull, foolish”), equivalent to German toll (“crazy”) and English dull. Sense 3 is a clipping of Aktendulli.

noun:Diversion.tx: Borrowed from Latin dīversiōnis, genitive of dīversio, verbal noun of dīverto.

phrase:denn man tau.tx: German Low German denn man tau, equivalent to standard German dann (“then”) mal (informal imperative modal particle) zu (“to”).

phrase:der Fall hat sich.tx: Literally, “the case has itself”. Ellipsis of a participle such as erledigt (“handled, concluded”).

adv:drauflos.tx: Univerbation of drauf + los. Compare Dutch erop los.

noun:Dörrfleisch.tx: From dörren (“to desiccate, to dry”) + Fleisch

phrase:die Einschläge kommen näher.tx: Literally, “the impacts are getting closer”. Compare English close to home. The idiomatic sense is first attested in the 1990s.

noun:Dressman.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from Dress + English man.

phrase:das Glück ist ein Vogerl.tx: Literally, “happiness is a litte bird”, from the Viennese song Das Glück is a Vogerl by Alexander von Biczò.

noun:Divergenz.tx: From divergieren + -enz. By surface analysis, divergent + -enz.
